Course Description

This course follows the history of the modern world from the First World War to our own day. In Quarter 3 you will study the Great War, the peace that followed it, the Depression, and the rise of the dictators who brought the world to war again. In Quarter 4 you will study the Second World War, the Cold War, the end of the European empires, the fall of the Soviet Union, and the world that came after.

There is no textbook. You will read two lessons each module, and you will read the words of the people who made these events: speeches, treaties, letters, laws, and reports. Primary sources are the center of the course. The lessons help you read them, and they raise questions that you answer yourself.

The course follows the Mississippi College- and Career-Readiness Standards for Social Studies, World History: Age of Enlightenment to Present.

What You Will Learn

  • Why the First World War began, how it was fought, and why the peace that ended it failed.
  • How the Great Depression, and the choices of a few men, led some nations into dictatorship and others through crisis with their freedom kept.
  • How the Second World War was won and lost, and what the victors did with their victory.
  • How the Cold War divided the world, why it never became a direct war between the two great powers, and how it ended.
  • How empires ended, how rights were claimed against states, and how oil, terror, and fast communication tied the modern world together.
  • How to read a primary source, weigh evidence, argue from it, and say honestly what the evidence cannot show.

How the Course Works

The course is built in modules, and each module is one week of work if you follow the suggested pace. Everything in a module carries its module number, so the second item in Module 20 is 20.2. Every module has the same parts:

ItemWhat it is
Introduction (.1)A short ungraded survey. You give your first answer to the module's question.
Lessons and primary sources (.3 to .6)Two lessons, each followed by a primary source. Read them in order.
Headline assignment (.7)The main graded work of the module. Its type changes from module to module.
Discussion (.8)A graded post on the module's question, with a reply to a classmate.
Review (.9)A short ungraded survey. You answer the module question again and tell your teacher how confident you feel and what is still unclear.
Quarter Exam (.10)In Modules 19 and 28 only. Twenty multiple-choice questions on that quarter.

Live and On-Demand students do the same work and are graded the same way. Live students meet with the class and teacher. On-Demand students work at their own pace within each quarter and should plan to finish each module before the next one opens.

Graded Work

Kind of workWhat it isPoints
Reading QuizSeven questions that ask you to work something out from the lessons and sources. Graded by Canvas.7
Primary Source ReportA report of 450 to 650 words in Word. Four questions, one of which asks what might have happened if one event had gone differently.16
Primary Source ExerciseFour questions typed in Canvas. One asks what might have happened if one event had gone differently.16
VR ActivityA solo session in your VR headset. Instructions appear in the module before it opens.10
CapstoneAn essay of 800 to 1,200 words at the end of each quarter. You choose one of three questions.20
DiscussionOne post of 150 to 250 words and one reply to a classmate.10
Quarter ExamTwenty multiple-choice questions on the modules of that quarter, at the end of Quarter 3 and Quarter 4.40
Introduction and Review surveysUngraded. They help your teacher see how the class is doing.0

Canvas keeps the work in five groups: Reading Quizzes, Discussions, Deep Feedback, Module Check-Ins, and Quarterly Exams. Your teacher decides how much each group counts toward your grade.

The two quarter exams together count for 30% of your grade. The rest is divided among the other groups: Reading Quizzes 7%, Discussions 31%, Deep Feedback 32%, and Module Check-Ins 0%.

[Teacher: if you change these weights in Canvas, update them here.]

How Your Writing Is Scored

Reports, exercises, and capstones are scored on four things, and the same four are used every time:

  • Understanding of the material: do you state the facts and the source's words accurately?
  • Quality of reasoning: do you build your claims from evidence and weigh other explanations?
  • Clarity and precision of expression: is your writing clear, organized, and exact?
  • Intellectual honesty: do you say what the source cannot show and what you cannot know?

You are graded on the quality of your argument, not on which side you take. Good arguments from different sides can both earn full credit.

Writing and Submitting in Microsoft 365

  • Write reports and capstones in Word, using your school Microsoft account.
  • Name each file like this: LastName_FirstName_AssignmentName_WHSP. For example, Smith_Jane_IsraelReport_WHSP.
  • Save your file in your OneDrive folder for this course, inside your History folder.
  • Submit from Canvas by choosing the OneDrive tab and selecting your file.
  • When a draft is required, save each draft as its own file. Do not overwrite an earlier one.
  • Put short quotations in quotation marks and cite each one in a footnote.

[Teacher: confirm the folder path and course code for your class.]

Primary Sources and Honest Scholarship

  • Quote the sources exactly and name where each quotation comes from.
  • Do not add details that the lessons and sources do not give. If you are guessing, say so.
  • When a question asks what might have happened, build your answer from the facts you know, and say what you cannot know.
  • Write about suffering and death plainly and with respect.
  • Your work must be your own. If you work in a group, the assignment tells you how to share the credit.

Group Work

In some modules the introduction survey lets you choose to work alone or with a group on the headline assignment. Students who choose a group agree to the Group Covenant and hand in one shared piece, with every member's name on it. Students who work alone do the same assignment and are scored the same way.

Your VR Sessions

Three modules include a solo session in your VR headset. Come to each session with your headset charged, your notebook, and the module's readings finished. Directions will appear in the module before it opens.

The Virtues in This Course

Every module asks you to think about people who needed courage, courtesy, honesty, perseverance, self-government, service, or responsibility, and about people who lacked them. The Review survey at the end of each module asks you to name one of these virtues and a person who needed it.

pages.title: Teacher's Manual 1: Start Here
pages.html:
This manual guides the teacher through every lesson, source, and graded item in Modules 11 to 28 (Quarters 3 and 4). Every entry opens with the standards benchmarks it satisfies. Modules, not weeks, are the governing order: everything in Module 20 is numbered 20.1, 20.3, and so on. Weeks appear only in the suggested schedule in Appendix B.

The shape of the course

  • Quarter 3, War and Dictatorship, is Modules 11 to 19 (World War I through the invasion of Poland), ending in the Quarter 3 Capstone. Quarter 4, World War and Cold War, is Modules 20 to 28 (World War II to the present), ending in the Quarter 4 Capstone.
  • Both sections, Live and On-Demand, use identical content and the same graded items.
  • Standards come from the Mississippi College- and Career-Readiness Standards for Social Studies, World History: Age of Enlightenment to Present. Benchmark 8.1 and Competencies 1 to 7 belong to Quarters 1 and 2. This manual covers 8.2 through 12.5.
  • There is no source textbook. Each module has two lessons and two paired primary sources. The narrative is Optima's own and rests on the sources.

What every module contains

NumberItemKind
N.1Module Introduction (survey)Tier 4, ungraded. Captures the student's first answer to the module question and, in Tier 3 weeks, the group opt-in.
N.2Module mapTier 4 overview page hosted on GitHub: the module question, a short ungraded check-in, what is ahead, what to turn in, and where to begin. Each map names one virtue to watch.
N.3 and N.5Lesson 1 and Lesson 2Tier 4 reading, hosted on GitHub and embedded in Canvas.
N.4 and N.6Primary Source 1 and 2Tier 4 reading, paired with the lesson before it.
N.7Headline assignmentOne per module. The type rotates: Reading Quiz, Primary Source Report, Primary Source Exercise, VR Activity, or Capstone.
N.8DiscussionTier 2. The module's essential question, 10 points.
N.9Module Review (survey)Tier 4, ungraded. Revisited answer, confidence rating, what is unclear, a virtue reflection, and a checklist of submissions.
N.10Quarter Exam (Modules 19 and 28 only)Twenty multiple-choice questions on that quarter alone, 2 points each, 40 points. It sits in the Quarterly Exams group.

Grading structure

Canvas holds five assignment groups: Reading Quizzes, Discussions, Deep Feedback, Module Check-Ins, and Quarterly Exams. Weighting is on. The two quarterly exams together carry 30%, the default for these courses. The other 70% is split in proportion to the points each group holds: Reading Quizzes 7%, Discussions 31%, Deep Feedback 32%, and Module Check-Ins 0%. All of these are yours to adjust. Appendix C gives the item counts, the shared rubric, and the time budget.

What to do before the course opens

  • Review the group weights in Canvas and adjust them if you wish.
  • Read the Group Covenant note in each Tier 3 module's introduction survey and make sure the covenant document is available to students.
  • Check the VR Activity items in Modules 16, 21, and 25. They are placeholders that say the activity design is pending.
  • Read Appendix D for primary-source texts that are still being verified.

How to use a module entry

Each entry lists the benchmarks at the top, the module question, the four readings with their benchmarks, the graded items with their groups and points, and grading guidance. Quiz entries include the answer key. Reports, exercises, and capstones include what a strong answer shows. Every report, exercise, and capstone contains a counterfactual. Grade the counterfactual on the quality of the argument, not on the conclusion.

pages.title: Module 11 Teacher Entry: The Marne and the Trenches
pages.html:
Quarter 3, Module 11, suggested Week 19.

Benchmarks satisfied

  • 8.2: Propaganda as a means of mobilizing civilians in World War I; the effect of prolonged trench warfare and attrition.

Module question

Could Germany have won in 1914?

Readings

ItemTitleBenchmarksNote
11.3Lesson 1: The Schlieffen Plan and the Marne8.2A war plan built on speed, and the days in September that broke it.
11.4Primary Source 1: Goschen's Report: The "Scrap of Paper"8.2A British ambassador's account of his last day in Berlin, August 4, 1914.
11.5Lesson 2: Trench War and Attrition: Ypres, Verdun, the Somme8.2How a war of movement became a war of endurance.
11.6Primary Source 2: Owen: "Dulce et Decorum Est"8.2A soldier-poet describes a gas attack on the Western Front.

Lesson objectives

  • Explain why Germany's war plan depended on speed and on crossing Belgium.
  • Trace the decisions that turned the German advance into a retreat at the Marne.
  • Argue, using specific decisions, whether Germany could have won in 1914.
  • Describe why trench warfare developed and what life in the trenches was like.
  • Compare the aims and results of Verdun and the Somme.
  • Explain how the idea of attrition shaped the way leaders fought the war.

Graded and survey items

ItemTypeTierCanvas groupPointsBenchmarks assessed
11.1Module IntroductionTier 4Module Check-Ins0Ungraded survey.
11.7Reading QuizTier 1Reading Quizzes78.2
11.8DiscussionTier 2Discussions108.2
11.9Module ReviewTier 4Module Check-Ins0Ungraded survey.

Reading Quiz answer key

#QuestionCorrect answerWhy
1Why did Schlieffen's plan send the main German army through Belgium instead of attacking France's border head-on?C. France's border was lined with strong forts, and a sweep through Belgium could trap the French armyFrance's frontier was heavily fortified, so Schlieffen planned to swing the right wing through Belgium and west of Paris and trap the French army against its own border. Belgium had promised nothing to Germany, and its army fought harder than Berlin expected.
2On August 1, 1914, the Kaiser asked whether the army could be sent east alone. Moltke said it could not. What does his answer show about the German war plan?A. Once it was set in motion it could not easily be changedMoltke said a million men could not be turned around on short notice. The plan was a timetable built on speed, with no room to change course.
3Which decision exposed the flank of the German First Army to Paris?D. Kluck's turn southeast to pass east of the cityOn September 2 Kluck, short of men and chasing the retreating Allies, turned southeast and passed east of Paris instead of west of it. That exposed his flank to the French army gathering in the city.
4In Goschen's report, how does Jagow's reason for entering Belgium differ from the reason Goschen gives for Britain's decision to go to war?B. Jagow calls it a matter of military need and speed, and Goschen calls it a matter of keeping a solemn promiseJagow says Germany had to go the quickest way, a matter of life and death. Goschen answers that it was a matter of life and death for Britain's honor to keep its solemn engagement.
5Why should a historian be careful about treating Goschen's report as proof of what the chancellor really thought?D. Goschen wrote for his own government and for the British public, and he chose what to put downThe dispatch was written days after the meeting, to Goschen's foreign minister, and published by the British government. It is a firsthand account, but from one side, and the writer chose what to include.
6Why did some commanders come to believe in attrition?A. Frontal attacks cost huge numbers of men and gained little, so they hoped to wear the enemy down until he could not fightAfter 1915 the generals saw that attacks gained almost no ground. Some concluded that the side with more men and factories would win if both sides lost men at the same rate.
7In "Dulce et Decorum Est," Owen calls the Latin line "the old Lie." What is he arguing?C. That a man who had seen a death by gas could not honestly tell children that dying for one's country is sweet and fittingOwen describes a man drowning in gas and tells the reader that, having seen it, no one could repeat the old line to children eager for glory. He wrote to change minds, which a historian must keep in view.

The quiz is auto-graded in Canvas (7 questions, 1 point each). Every question asks for an inference across the lessons, not a look-up.

Discussion

This week's question: Could Germany have won in 1914? Choose a side. In your answer, name at least two specific decisions made between 1905 and September 1914, and explain how each one could have gone another way. Write 150 to 250 words. State one claim you believe is true. Then explain why, using the specific evidence named above. Keep to what the lessons and the sources show. If you are guessing, say so.

Score with the 10-point rubric: 6 points for the claim and its evidence, 4 for the reply to a classmate. Substantive is full credit, thin is partial, missing is zero. Post two or three short public comments that model good reasoning.

Module question

May a free state silence dissent in wartime?

  • Evaluate whether limits on speech helped or harmed the free states that adopted them.

Primary Source Report: questions and what a strong answer shows

#QuestionLook for
1Who was Schenck, what did his leaflet say, and what test does Justice Holmes announce? Explain "clear and present danger" and "proximity and degree" in your own words.Strong answers state the leaflet's aim and define the test in the student's own words, not by repeating Holmes's phrases.

What does he assume about the freedom of a free people when their nation is at war?Holmes assumes that the protection of speech depends on circumstances and that war changes them. Credit answers that say so and then ask whether the assumption is sound.

Weak answers only list similarities.

Primary Source Exercise: questions and what a strong answer shows

#QuestionLook for
1What does Wilson say the United States wants from the war, and what does he say it does not want? Why would it matter in 1917 for him to say "We desire no conquest, no dominion"?Wilson's aims: no conquest, no dominion, a war for democracy. Credit an explanation of why a public denial of gain mattered in 1917.
2Wilson speaks of "the German people" and "the German Government" as two different things. What idea about who is responsible for a war does this assume, and what does it let him say?The distinction between a people and its government assumes that rulers, not peoples, answer for a war. It lets Wilson fight Germany's government while claiming friendship for its people.
3Lenin refuses "the slightest concession to 'revolutionary defencism.'" Use Lesson 2 to explain how a program like this helped take Russia out of the war. Then name one other cause of Russia's exit that Lenin did not control.Lenin's program of peace without concessions fed the exhaustion in Russian armies. A second cause might be the army's collapse or the failures of the Provisional Government.
4Choose ONE. (a) Suppose Germany had never sent the Zimmermann Telegram. (b) Suppose Germany had never let Lenin cross Germany in 1917. Explain how the war might have gone differently, and what evidence from the lessons supports your guess. Then say what makes your guess uncertain.Counterfactual. The student chooses (a) or (b). Credit evidence from Lesson 2 or Lesson 1 tied to the guess and a plain statement of its uncertainty.

#QuestionCorrect answerWhy
1After the killings of 1927, why was Mao's turn to the countryside a sensible choice for the Communists who survived?B. Nine in ten Chinese lived in the countryside, Chiang held the cities, and the peasants had gained little under his ruleChiang's power rested on the cities, and the countryside, where nine in ten Chinese lived, was left much as before. Mao argued that peasants could make a revolution. The Soviet advisers had taught the opposite, so Moscow did not order it.
2The fifth encirclement campaign forced the Communists out of Jiangxi. What made it different from the earlier campaigns?D. Chiang's armies built lines of small forts and cut off the Communists' food, so the Red Army could no longer slip awayFollowing a German adviser's plan, Chiang's armies built lines of small forts and cut off food. 3What was the most important result of Zhang Xueliang's arrest of Chiang at Xi'an in December 1936?A. It ended Chiang's plan to crush the Communists first and led to a second united front against JapanChiang came out alive after two weeks and agreed to a second united front, so when Japan attacked in 1937 the two parties fought on the same side. Zhang was the one held under guard for most of his long life.
4By law the army and navy ministers in Japan had to be serving officers. What did this rule allow the military to do?C. Bring down any cabinet it disliked by having its minister resign, so civil leaders could never fully control the armyIf the military disliked a cabinet, its minister could resign and the cabinet would fall. That gave the army a veto over civil government long before it seized open control.
5The lesson notes that after the Mukden bomb a train passed over the spot soon afterward. Why does the lesson include this detail?A. It suggests the explosion was too slight to be a real attack, which fits the later finding that Japanese officers set the bomb themselvesA bomb that could not stop a train was a poor excuse for an invasion. The detail supports what we now know, that officers of the Kwantung Army staged the incident. The lesson does not say Tokyo ordered it; the government told the army to stop.
6The Lytton Report judged that Japan's attack was not self-defense. What does what happened next show?D. That a body can judge an aggressor correctly and still have no means to enforce its verdictThe League accepted the report in February 1933. Japan simply walked out and later left the League, and the great powers did nothing. The report was careful and fair, but the League had no force behind it.
7Mao writes, "the Party commands the gun, and the gun must never be allowed to command the Party." Why would a student who has just read about Japan notice this sentence?B. It names the danger Japan had fallen into, an army that answers to no civil authority, and says his party must prevent itIn Japan junior officers forced the government to follow them, and violence was rewarded. Mao names the same problem from the other side. His sentence also says political power grows out of the gun, so he does not reject force, only an army that rules its masters.

#QuestionCorrect answerBenchmarksWhy
1Why did German planners want to beat France quickly and then turn east?C. Russia needed weeks to mobilize, so Germany could win in the west first8.2Lesson 1 of Module 11: Russia's railways were thin, so its army was slow, which gave Germany a short window to win in the west and then face the east.
2On September 2, 1914, General von Kluck turned southeast and passed east of Paris. What did this do?A. It exposed his flank to the French army gathering in Paris8.2French pilots spotted the move, and the new French army struck the flank on September 5. This led to the Battle of the Marne.
3Why did the Allies attack the Dardanelles and Gallipoli in 1915?D. To knock the Ottoman Empire out of the war and open a sea road to Russia8.2, 8.5Russia was nearly cut off from its allies while the straits were closed. The plan was meant to go around the trenches.
4What does Lesson 1 of Module 12 say about the Bryce Report of 1915?B. It was based on real killings, but some of its worst stories had weak evidence8.2, 8.5Later historians confirmed the killings but found that some tales, such as mutilated children, had little support.
5Why did the Zimmermann Telegram turn American opinion against Germany?B. It offered Mexico help to win back Texas and other lands, and Zimmermann admitted it8.3The offer was not realistic, but Americans in the West and South now saw danger on their own border. Zimmermann's admission ended doubts that it was a forgery.
6What did the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk cost Russia?D. Poland, the Baltic lands, Ukraine, and a third of its people8.3, 9.5Lesson 2 of Module 13 also says Russia lost much of its coal, iron, and farmland. It calls this a victor's peace of just the kind Wilson said the world should not impose.
7What did Article 231 of the Treaty of Versailles say?A. Germany and its allies were responsible for all loss and damage8.4, 8.5Germans called it the war guilt clause. It was the basis for reparations, which were set at 132 billion gold marks in 1921.
8Why did the United States Senate refuse to approve the Treaty of Versailles?C. Senators feared Article 10 could send soldiers to war without a vote of Congress, and Wilson would not bargain8.4A small group opposed any League, and a larger group wanted only small changes. Wilson's refusal to compromise kept the middle group from joining him.
9What was John Maynard Keynes's main argument in The Economic Consequences of the Peace?D. The reparations were too large to pay and would drag down all of Europe8.4, 9.1Later historians said he exaggerated, but the book shaped opinion in Britain and America and made the treaty harder to enforce.
10Why was Mussolini able to take power in October 1922?B. The King would not use the army against the march and asked Mussolini to lead9.2The Fascists had won only 35 of 535 seats in 1921. The march became a victory parade because the one man who could stop it chose not to.
11Who suffered most from the German hyperinflation of 1923, according to Lesson 2 of Module 15?A. People who had saved for years, such as retired teachers9.3Those who owed money paid their debts in worthless paper, while savers lost everything. Many of these middle-class families lost faith in the republic.
12In his postscript of January 4, 1923, what did Lenin say about Stalin?C. He was too rude and should be replaced as General Secretary by a more patient man9.2, 9.5Lenin wrote this after Stalin shouted at his wife, Krupskaya. The Testament was kept from the public until the 1950s.
13Why did the poor harvest of 1932 become a famine that killed millions?D. The state kept its grain quotas and seized seed and food from villages9.2, 9.5The government also set roadblocks to stop starving peasants from leaving. Historians estimate that five to seven million died, and no one disputes that its decisions turned a bad harvest into mass death.
14How did the vote on the Enabling Act of March 23, 1933, pass?B. Communist deputies were jailed or in hiding, SA men stood outside, and the Center Party voted yes9.2, 10.1The vote was 444 to 94, and only the Social Democrats voted no. It was a lawful act that ended the rule of law.
15How did Hitler become Chancellor on January 30, 1933?A. Papen persuaded Hindenburg to appoint him, believing he could be controlled9.2, 10.1The cabinet held only three Nazis, and the Nazi vote had actually fallen in November 1932. Papen is reported to have said, "We have hired him."
16Why did Mao's Communists begin the Long March in October 1934?C. Chiang's forts cut off their food and the Jiangxi Soviet began to starve9.5Chiang's fifth campaign used lines of small forts. About eighty-six thousand broke out of the ring and marched some six thousand miles, and perhaps ten thousand reached Shaanxi.
17What do we now know about the bomb on the railway near Mukden in September 1931?B. Japanese officers set it themselves as an excuse to attack9.5bThe damage was so slight that a train crossed the spot soon after. Within months the army had overrun Manchuria, and the government in Tokyo did not dare punish it.
18Who was NOT invited to the Munich conference of September 1938?D. Czechoslovakia and the Soviet Union, whose fate was being decided10.1Only Hitler, Mussolini, Chamberlain, and Daladier took part. The Sudetenland went to Germany, and Czechoslovakia lost its forts and much of its industry.
19Why did Stalin sign the Nazi-Soviet Pact in August 1939?A. He distrusted the West after Munich and wanted time to build up his army10.1Britain and France sent only a low-ranking mission by slow boat, and Poland and Romania would not let Soviet troops cross. Stalin also gained land, and Hitler could attack Poland without a war on two fronts.
20Britain's promise to defend Poland in March 1939 was remarkable. Why?C. Britain had never before guaranteed borders in eastern Europe, and had no army to send10.1It was meant as a warning that this time Britain might fight. Britain also began a peacetime draft in April.

#QuestionCorrect answerWhy
1The best French and British armies moved north into Belgium when the Germans attacked on May 10. Why did this help the German plan?C. 2The lesson says the Allies had about as many tanks as the Germans, and many of theirs were better built. What actually made the difference?A. The French spread their tanks among the infantry, while the Germans massed theirs, gave them radios, and backed them with aircraftThe lesson notes what did not decide the matter. The difference was in how the tanks were used, in groups, with radios and air cover. A weapon is only as good as the plan that uses it.
3Lord Halifax declined to become prime minister on May 10, 1940, and Churchill took the post. Why does the lesson tell you to notice how narrow the choice was?D. A different answer from one man on one afternoon would have given Britain a different leader, which shows how much can turn on a single decisionThe lesson is making a point about contingency. Halifax wanted to see what terms Hitler would offer, and a cabinet led by him might well have taken a settlement. 4Why do historians still argue about the German tanks' halt before Dunkirk on May 24?B. What is not in doubt is the result. The pause gave the British two days to strengthen the ring around the port.
5Crowds welcomed the soldiers home from Dunkirk as winners. Why did Churchill say that "wars are not won by evacuations"?D. He wanted to warn the country that the army was saved but its guns and tanks were not, and that the war was still to be wonChurchill's speech, in the second primary source, says the rescue must not be given the marks of a victory. The army came home with its rifles but not its equipment. He then moves at once to a promise never to surrender, so the two claims fit together.

The airfields had been near their limit, and the pause let Fighter Command recover and fight onBy early September the airfields were near the limit. When the Luftwaffe turned to London, the pilots and fields had time to recover. On September 15 the Luftwaffe lost many planes, and Hitler put Sea Lion off.

1At Yalta the Western leaders won a promise of free elections in Poland. Critics say Roosevelt gave Eastern Europe away, and defenders say he gave nothing. pages.title: Module 27 Teacher Entry: The Soviet Collapse
pages.html:
Quarter 4, Module 27, suggested Week 35.

Benchmarks satisfied

  • 11.1: Economic, political, and military shifts of the Cold War era: the Truman Doctrine and Marshall Plan in Europe and Southeast Asia, nationalism in Africa and the Middle East, detente in China, and the fall of Communism in the Soviet Union.
  • 11.5: The collapse of the Soviet Union and Russia's struggle for democracy: perestroika, glasnost, Gorbachev, Reagan, and Yeltsin.

Module question

Did Reagan win the Cold War, or did the Soviet Union lose it?

Readings

ItemTitleBenchmarksNote
27.3Lesson 1: Detente, Afghanistan, Reagan, and Solidarity11.1, 11.5How the Cold War eased, grew hard again, and began to crack from within the Soviet bloc.
27.4Primary Source 1: Reagan, Address at the Brandenburg Gate (June 12, 1987)11.1, 11.5The American president speaks beside the Berlin Wall and addresses the Soviet leader.
27.5Lesson 2: Gorbachev, 1989, and the End of the Soviet Union11.1, 11.5How reform from above and revolt from below ended the Soviet empire without a war.
27.6Primary Source 2: Gorbachev, Resignation Address (December 25, 1991)11.1, 11.5The last Soviet leader ends the Soviet Union in a few minutes on television.

Lesson objectives

  • Explain what detente achieved and what it did not.
  • Describe the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan and the American response.
  • Explain the rise of Solidarity in Poland and how Reagan's policies changed the Cold War.
  • Explain what Gorbachev tried to reform and why it did not work as he hoped.
  • Describe how the Communist governments of Eastern Europe fell in 1989.
  • Explain how the Soviet Union itself came to an end in 1991.

Source note: Primary Source 2: translation to confirm.

Reading Quiz answer key

#QuestionCorrect answerWhy
1The Soviets wanted the Helsinki Final Act of 1975 because it recognized the borders set after the war. Why did it turn out to work against them?D. Its pledge to respect human rights gave dissidents in Moscow, Prague, and Warsaw a standard by which to judge their governmentsThe lesson says the Soviets thought they had won, but the human-rights pledge gave courage to dissidents, who formed groups to watch whether their governments kept the promise.
2In December 1980 the Soviet leaders discussed invading Poland and decided against it. Which reason does the lesson give?A. Afghanistan was already costing the Soviet Union too muchThe lesson says the Soviet leaders decided against invasion because Afghanistan was already costing too much. Poland's own general later declared martial law instead.
3John Paul II visited Poland in June 1979, and many Poles said afterward that it changed how they saw themselves. According to the lesson, what did they see?C. How many of them there were, and that they were not aloneThe lesson says millions came out to see him, and for the first time many Poles saw how many of them there were. That is what a free union needed in 1980.
4General Jaruzelski declared martial law in December 1981 and banned Solidarity. What does the lesson say this showed?B. That the government could rule by force but not by consent, and that the union survived underground with the help of the ChurchPoland was kept quiet but not conquered. Solidarity's members went underground and the Church sheltered them. The lesson says the government learned it could rule by force but not by consent.
5Reagan said, "Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!" The wall stood for two more years. Which reading of the speech does the excerpt best support?D. It welcomed some of what Gorbachev had done and asked for one clear public act, so it offered a way forward as well as a demandThe excerpt welcomes "change and openness" and then names one sign that would be unmistakable. The wall did not fall until November 1989, so the speech did not cause it by itself.
6Gorbachev meant glasnost to help the Communist Party. Why does the lesson say it worked against him?B. It showed the Party's crimes and failures, as at Chernobyl, so that many citizens stopped trusting what they were toldThe government hid the facts of Chernobyl for days. When the truth came out, trust fell. The lesson says the reforms weakened the old system without building a new one that worked.
7A student argues that the Soviet empire in Eastern Europe fell because its rulers chose not to use force. Which evidence from Lesson 2 best supports this?A. At Leipzig the police were ready to fire on seventy thousand marchers and did not, and Soviet troops stayed in their barracks, while in Beijing the rulers sent tanks into Tiananmen Square and kept powerThe lesson calls the decision not to use force the hinge in Eastern Europe. China is the contrast: its rulers used force and survived. The other choices are true, but none of them is about a choice to use or withhold force.

The quiz is auto-graded in Canvas (7 questions, 1 point each). Every question asks for an inference across the lessons, not a look-up.

Discussion

This week's question: Did Reagan win the Cold War, or did the Soviet Union lose it? Choose one answer. Use your list of pressures. Name one pressure from outside and one from within that bear on your answer, with the dates and the people involved. Then take up the choice at Leipzig and Beijing in 1989. Say what might have followed if the men in Moscow had used force, as the men in Beijing did. Write 150 to 250 words. State one claim you believe is true. Then explain why, using the specific evidence named above. Keep to what the lessons and the sources show. If you are guessing, say so.

Score with the 10-point rubric: 6 points for the claim and its evidence, 4 for the reply to a classmate. Substantive is full credit, thin is partial, missing is zero. Post two or three short public comments that model good reasoning.

pages.title: Module 28 Teacher Entry: A Smaller World: Quarter 4 Capstone
pages.html:
Quarter 4, Module 28, suggested Week 36.

Benchmarks satisfied

  • 12.1: Issues that advanced civil and human rights, including Mandela and Martin Luther King Jr., and humanitarian military engagements in Kosovo and Bosnia.
  • 12.2: OPEC's dominance of the oil market and its influence on Middle Eastern foreign policy: embargoes, the Iranian Hostage Crisis, and the Gulf Wars.
  • 12.3: Modern domestic and global terrorism: the September 11 attack, the War in Afghanistan, and the rise of ISIS.
  • 12.4: Global reactions to immigration, national deficits, and anti-austerity movements, including the Arab Spring, Brexit, and the election of Donald Trump.
  • 12.5: Modern technology as a prompter of immediate reactions to government policies, and the influence of social media.

Module question

Does a smaller world make free peoples safer or more exposed?

Readings

ItemTitleBenchmarksNote
28.3Lesson 1: Moral Claims Against State Power: Mandela, King, and the Balkans12.1How three struggles tested what a people may do when its own government wrongs it, and what others may do about it.

Lesson objectives

  • Explain how apartheid ended and why Mandela turned to armed struggle before he sought peace.
  • Explain how King argued that unjust laws could be resisted, and compare his method with Mandela's.
  • Describe how Yugoslavia broke apart and how the world responded.
  • Explain why oil gave the Middle East such weight in world affairs after 1973.
  • Describe the rise of al-Qaeda, the attacks of September 11, 2001, and the American response.
  • Explain how the internet and satellite news changed the speed at which events and ideas spread.

Capstone: framing questions and what strong essays show

  • Question 1 asks why the superpowers never fought directly. Strong essays weigh leaders, nuclear fear, and luck, and use the Cuban missile crisis.
  • Question 2 asks what a people may do when its government wrongs it and what other nations may do. Strong essays use at least two cases from the quarter and name the costs of each means.

Students choose one question and write 800 to 1,200 words in Word, submitted from OneDrive. The essay must use evidence from four different weeks, quote two primary sources with footnotes, include a counterfactual, answer the strongest objection, and state what the evidence cannot show. Score with the four-criterion rubric (20 points, 5 per criterion). Both the group and the individual path use the same rubric.

Discussion

This week's question: Does a smaller world make free peoples safer or more exposed? Choose one answer. Use your two lists. Name two items from the lists, with dates, that support your answer. Then name one item that belongs on both lists, and explain how the same thing can make a free people stronger and weaker at once. Write 150 to 250 words. State one claim you believe is true. Then explain why, using the specific evidence named above. Write plainly and with respect about the people who died on September 11 and in the wars that followed. Keep to what the lessons and the sources show. If you are guessing, say so.

Score with the 10-point rubric: 6 points for the claim and its evidence, 4 for the reply to a classmate. Substantive is full credit, thin is partial, missing is zero. Post two or three short public comments that model good reasoning.

Quarter 4 Exam answer key

#QuestionCorrect answerBenchmarksWhy
1In May 1940 the best French and British armies moved north into Belgium. Why was this a mistake?B. It was what the German plan wanted, with the main thrust in the Ardennes10.1The sichelschnitt plan cut off the armies that had gone north. The lesson says the Allies had about as many tanks, but the Germans massed theirs, gave them radios, and backed them with aircraft.
2Why did Winston Churchill become prime minister on May 10, 1940?D. Chamberlain resigned after the failure in Norway and Lord Halifax declined the post10.1Halifax said that a peer in the House of Lords would find it hard to lead the war. The lesson says a different answer from one man that afternoon would have given Britain a different leader.
3Why did Japan's leaders decide in 1941 to go to war with the United States?A. An oil embargo threatened their fleet, and they would not leave China10.1, 10.2Japan had almost no oil of its own, and its navy had about eighteen months of fuel. The American note of November 26 asked Japan to leave China and Indochina, and Japan's leaders took it as a final demand.
4How did the Americans know to wait for the Japanese at Midway?C. Codebreakers read the Japanese code and learned that the target "AF" was Midway10.1, 10.2Commander Rochefort's team made the reading, and a plain-language message about a broken water plant proved that AF was Midway. Nimitz trusted it, moved his three carriers, and had the damaged Yorktown patched in three days.
5How was the German Sixth Army trapped at Stalingrad?B. Soviet armies broke the Romanian flanks, and Hitler refused to let Paulus break out10.2The Soviets struck on November 19, and about 250,000 men were caught. Paulus surrendered on February 2, 1943, and only a few thousand of the 91,000 prisoners ever came home.
6According to Lesson 2 of Module 22, what was the Wannsee Conference?D. The moment when state officials agreed to organize killing already under way10.2, 10.3Mass murder had already begun with the shootings in the east. The minutes use plain, official words that hid the crime, and the clerks were as necessary to it as the guards.
7The Potsdam Declaration of July 1945 called on Japan to surrender. What did it leave unsaid?A. What would become of the emperor10.3, 10.4It repeated the demand for unconditional surrender and did not say what would happen to the emperor. Historians still argue over what Japan meant by the word mokusatsu.
8How did the Nuremberg tribunal answer the charge that crimes against peace were an ex post facto law?C. Germany had signed the Kellogg-Briand Pact of 1928 giving up war10.3, 10.4The old rule says no one may be punished for something that was not a crime when it was done. The tribunal said justice would be poorly served if the guilty went free on a technicality, though some American leaders, such as Senator Taft, still thought the principle had been broken.
9Why does each permanent member of the UN Security Council hold a veto?B. The great powers would not join without it, so it limits the UN10.4The lesson says the founders were realistic, since peace could not be kept by a body that the strongest states would not obey.
10Why did the Western powers introduce a new currency, the Deutsche Mark, in June 1948?D. To stop inflation and restart trade in the Western zones11.1, 11.2, 11.3The Soviets answered on June 24 by cutting the road, rail, and canal links to West Berlin.
11Why was the Warsaw Pact formed in May 1955?A. West Germany had joined NATO five days earlier11.1, 11.2, 11.3The Soviet Union and seven satellite states signed. Europe now had two armed blocs, and the Iron Curtain ran through the middle of Germany.
12Why could the Soviet Union not veto the United Nations vote to defend South Korea in 1950?C. Its delegate was boycotting the Council over the seating of China11.3, 11.4The Security Council voted to defend South Korea. Truman took the matter to the United Nations and did not wait for Congress.
13What was the secret part of the bargain that ended the Cuban missile crisis?B. The American Jupiter missiles in Turkey would be removed within a few months11.3, 11.4Robert Kennedy told the Soviet ambassador in secret. The Jupiters left Turkey in the spring of 1963, and for many years the public did not know.
14Why did the partition of India in 1947 lead to such suffering?C. A judge who had never been to India drew the borders in about five weeks9.4Mountbatten had moved the date forward, and Radcliffe drew the line in haste. Ten to fifteen million people crossed it, and the lesson asks you to notice how much depended on a few men and a rushed schedule.
15Why did Britain and France stop their attack on Egypt on November 6, 1956?B. Eisenhower opposed it and the United States refused to help the British pound9.4, 10.3, 11.4Eisenhower was furious that he had not been told, and he would not accept an invasion of a Third World nation by his allies. Soviet tanks were crushing the Hungarian revolt at the same time.
16Which pair correctly names Gorbachev's two policies?A. Perestroika, which restructured the economy, and glasnost, which allowed criticism and free speech11.1, 11.5Gorbachev wished to save communism, not end it. Both policies weakened the old system without building a new one that worked.
17How did the Berlin Wall open on November 9, 1989?D. A spokesman misread his notes on travel rules, and guards with no orders opened the gates11.1, 11.5Crowds poured to the wall that night. It was one of many moments in 1989 when a government chose not to use force.
18How did the coup against Gorbachev in August 1991 fail?B. Yeltsin called the people to resist, and the army would not fire11.5Yeltsin stood on a tank in front of the Russian parliament. The coup fell apart in three days. Gorbachev came back, but the power was gone, and in December the Soviet Union ended.
19Which statement about Mandela's presidency fits Lesson 1 of Module 28?C. His government set up a Truth and Reconciliation Commission, and he served one term12.1He stepped down in 1999. The lesson says that he did not take revenge and did not cling to power, and calls this the virtue of magnanimity.
20After the September 11 attacks, NATO did something it had never done before. What was it?D. It treated the attack on one member as an attack on all12.3NATO's Article 5 had never before been used. In October 2001 American and allied forces entered Afghanistan.

The exam covers this quarter only. It has 20 multiple-choice questions at 2 points each and is graded by Canvas.

Canvas weighting is on. The two quarterly exams carry 30% together, which is the default for these courses. The other 70% is split in proportion to the points each group holds. The weights are yours to adjust in Canvas.

The shared rubric

Primary Source Reports, Primary Source Exercises, and Capstones use four criteria in the same order: understanding of the material, quality of reasoning, clarity and precision of expression, and intellectual honesty. Reports and Exercises give each criterion 4 points (16 total). Capstones give 5 (20 total). Each has four levels: excellent, proficient, developing, beginning.

Discussion rubric

Ten points: 6 for the claim and its evidence, 4 for the reply to a classmate. Substantive earns full credit, thin earns half, missing earns zero.

Time budget

  • Tier 1: no teacher time. The quiz grades itself.
  • Tier 2: read the discussion in batches, score by rubric, and post two or three public comments. Budget about 30 seconds a post. Triage the Review survey in 15 to 20 minutes a module.
  • Tier 3: one headline per module at most. A Report, Exercise, or Capstone takes about five minutes per submission with the rubric. Capstones deserve a few more.
  • VR placeholders take no teacher time until the activity is designed.

Group work

In the modules that offer it (Modules 12, 13, 14, 17, 19, 22, 23, 26, 28), the introduction survey asks whether the student will work alone or with a group. Group students sign the Group Covenant and submit one shared piece with all names listed. Both paths use the same rubric.

Submissions through OneDrive

Reports and Capstones are Word documents. Students save the file in their OneDrive course folder and submit through the OneDrive tab. The file name pattern is LastName_FirstName_AssignmentName_WHSP. The course code and folder path are provisional and should be set to your own.

SUPPLEMENT A · PRIMARY SOURCE EXERCISE
The Depression and the Good Neighbor
Roosevelt turns away from armed intervention in Latin America.
📝 THE TASK

By 1933 the United States had sent troops into several lands of Central America and the Caribbean to protect its money, its citizens, and its canal. The Marines left Nicaragua in January 1933, and the long occupation of Haiti ended in 1934. Then the Great Depression came. World trade fell, and Latin American nations could not sell their sugar, coffee, and metals. Many could not pay their debts. Franklin Roosevelt took office in March 1933 and wanted friends and markets to the south.

On December 26, 1933, at a conference in Montevideo, Uruguay, the American nations signed a treaty saying that no state has the right to intervene in the affairs of another. The United States signed it with some reservations. Two days later Roosevelt spoke in Washington to the Woodrow Wilson Foundation.

Read the passages below. Three words may be new: “resolutely” means with firm purpose, “sanctity” means holy or sacred worth, and “intervention” means stepping into another nation’s affairs.

“In the field of world policy I would dedicate this nation to the policy of the good neighbor, the neighbor who resolutely respects himself and, because he does so, respects the rights of others, the neighbor who respects his obligations and respects the sanctity of his agreements in and with a world of neighbors.”

[...]

“The definite policy of the United States from now on is one opposed to armed intervention.”

Franklin D. Roosevelt, First Inaugural Address, March 4, 1933, and address to the Woodrow Wilson Foundation, December 28, 1933. Public-domain texts of United States government speeches. Sovereignty, Borders, and Debt
Two leaders of 2013 and 2017 argue that nations should govern themselves first.
